title: Expiry, eviction and memory
goal: By the end you can say when an expired key really leaves memory, predict what a full Redis does under each eviction policy, and choose a TTL, a maxmemory and a policy for a payment service's Redis.

warmup.q: A batch job wrote 500,000 idempotency keys with `EX 3`. Three seconds later a client sends `GET idem:250000`. What does it get, and is the key's memory free yet?
options: The old value: Redis deletes expired keys only once a second, in a sweep
nil, and the memory of all 500,000 keys is already free
nil, but most of the 500,000 keys are still in memory for about another second
nil only after `SCAN` has visited the key
warmup.why: Every command checks a key's deadline before it runs, so the GET deletes that one key and answers nil. The other keys are removed by a cycle that runs 10 times a second in slices of at most 25 ms. On the lab server it needed about 1.1 seconds to reclaim all 500,000. There is no once-a-second sweep that could return a stale value, and `SCAN` plays no part.

sections.h: A TTL is a deadline Redis keeps with the key
sections.body:
An idempotency key protects one card payment from being charged twice. Your service stores `idem:7f3a` when the request arrives, and a client that retries within the next 24 hours finds it and gets the first answer back. After that the key is garbage. At 35 payments a second, that is 3 million new keys a day.

Without help from the server you would clean up yourself: store the creation time inside each value, and run a job that walks every key with `SCAN` (lesson 2's page-by-page cursor) and deletes the old ones. That job reads 3 million keys a day on lesson 1's single thread (the one thread that runs every command, one at a time), and any key it misses stays forever.

So Redis lets you give a key a deadline. `SET idem:7f3a pending EX 86400` stores the value and says "delete this 86,400 seconds from now". Redis turns that into an absolute time, a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, and keeps it with the key. It also keeps a second index that holds only the keys that have a deadline, and `INFO keyspace` shows both counts: `keys=2,expires=1`. The time a key has left is its **TTL**, time to live. `TTL` reports it in seconds, `PTTL` in milliseconds, and `EXPIRETIME` returns the deadline itself.

That picture is the model for this lesson. Redis gets rid of keys in two ways. Expiry removes keys whose deadline has passed. Eviction removes keys that Redis chooses itself when memory is full. Both run on the same single thread, between and before your commands, and the rest of the lesson fills in how.

A few rules cause most TTL bugs:

- A plain `SET` replaces the value and drops the TTL, so the key now lives forever. Add `KEEPTTL` (Redis 6.0) to keep the old deadline. Commands that change a value in place, such as `INCR`, `HSET` or `RPUSH`, keep it.
- `EXPIRE` on a key that already has a TTL replaces the deadline. Since Redis 7.0 it takes `NX` (only if there is no TTL yet), `XX` (only if there is one), `GT` (only if the new deadline is later) and `LT` (only if it is earlier).
- `PERSIST` removes the TTL. `TTL` answers -1 for a key without one, and -2 for a key that doesn't exist.
- A TTL belongs to a whole key. To expire single fields of a hash, Redis 7.4 added `HEXPIRE`.

try.title: Set, keep and lose a TTL
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the server if it isn't running (`docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d`) and open a prompt with `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli`.
Type the commands below one at a time. Before the second `TTL idem:7f3a`, predict what a plain `SET` did to the deadline.
Before each `EXPIRE ... GT` and `EXPIRE ... NX`, predict whether it changes anything. It returns 1 when it did and 0 when it didn't.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.src:
SET idem:7f3a pending EX 86400
TTL idem:7f3a
PTTL idem:7f3a
SET idem:7f3a done
TTL idem:7f3a
SET idem:7f3a done EX 86400
SET idem:7f3a settled KEEPTTL
TTL idem:7f3a
INCR auths:card:7
EXPIRE auths:card:7 60
INCR auths:card:7
TTL auths:card:7
EXPIRE auths:card:7 30 GT
EXPIRE auths:card:7 600 GT
EXPIRE auths:card:7 10 NX
PERSIST auths:card:7
TTL auths:card:7
TTL no:such:key
INFO keyspace

try.expect: The first `TTL` prints `(integer) 86400` and `PTTL` about `(integer) 86399999`. After the plain `SET idem:7f3a done`, `TTL` prints `(integer) -1`: the key now lives forever. `SET ... KEEPTTL` keeps the deadline, so the next `TTL` is back near 86400. `INCR` keeps the 60-second TTL that `EXPIRE` set, so `TTL auths:card:7` still prints `(integer) 60`. `EXPIRE ... 30 GT` returns `(integer) 0` (30 s is not later than 60 s) and `EXPIRE ... 600 GT` returns `(integer) 1`. `EXPIRE ... NX` returns 0 because the key already has a TTL. After `PERSIST`, `TTL` is -1; for a missing key it is -2. `INFO keyspace` ends with `db0:keys=2,expires=1,...`: two keys, one of them in the expires index.

sections.h: Expired keys die on access, and by sampling
sections.body:
The 3 million idempotency keys from the last section each have their own deadline, somewhere in the next 24 hours, and Redis has to delete each one at about the right moment, on one thread.

The obvious design is a timer per key. Three million timers cost memory, and they would all fire on the one thread. The next idea is a sweep: once a second, check every key that has a deadline. That is 3 million comparisons every second, and while the sweep runs no client is served, because it runs on the same thread as every command.

Redis does two cheap things instead.

The first is **lazy expiry**. Every command that touches a key checks the key's deadline first. If the deadline has passed, Redis deletes the key right there and behaves as if it had never existed. That costs one comparison per access, and it guarantees that no client ever reads an expired value. On its own it leaks memory: most idempotency keys are written once and never read again, so nothing would ever look at them.

The second is **active expiry**, a cycle on the main thread. Ten times a second (the `hz` setting, 10 by default), it walks the expires index from where it stopped last time, checks 20 keys and deletes the expired ones. If more than 10% of that batch had expired, there is probably more to do, so it takes another batch at once. It stops when a batch comes back mostly clean, or when it has used 25 ms, a quarter of the 100 ms between runs. A few expired keys cost almost nothing. Many get the thread's full attention, in slices short enough that clients are still served in between.

So an expired key becomes invisible at once, and leaves memory a little later. The lab server showed both with 500,000 idempotency keys that shared one deadline. A GET returned nil in the first poll after the deadline, and that GET deleted exactly one key: the expired count went from 0 to 1 while `DBSIZE` still said 500,001. The cycle then removed about 400,000 keys a second, and memory fell from 40 MB to 2 MB in about 1.1 seconds. Those deletions are main-thread work, so a mass expiry is a latency bump for every client. Lesson 5 shows how to spread deadlines out.

`INFO stats` keeps the score: `expired_keys` counts every expiry, `expired_keys_active` the cycle's share, and `expired_time_cap_reached_count` the runs that hit the 25 ms limit. Replicas never expire keys on their own. They wait for the primary to send a `DEL` (lesson 10), and until it arrives they answer reads for an expired key with nil, like the primary.

sections.h: With a maxmemory limit, a full Redis refuses writes by default
sections.body:
Expiry only removes keys that have a deadline. A cache whose entries have no TTL, or a write rate that outruns the TTLs, keeps growing. By default nothing stops it: on 64-bit systems `maxmemory` is 0, which means no limit. Redis grows until it reaches the memory limit of its container or VM, and then the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer ends the process. In Docker you see exit code 137. Every client loses its connection at once, and a Redis without persistence comes back empty.

The fix is to give Redis a budget: `maxmemory 4gb` in the config file, or `CONFIG SET maxmemory 4gb` while it runs. Before Redis runs a command that can add data (`SET`, `HSET`, `LPUSH`, `INCR` and many more), it compares its memory use with the limit. Under the limit, the command runs. Over it, the **eviction policy** decides what happens.

The default policy is `noeviction`: refuse the write with an error and keep every key. The lab's small server has a 4 MB limit and already uses 1.41 MB when it is empty. About 2,300 values of 1 KB fit, and then the next write fails:

```text
(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
```

Reads keep working, and so do `DEL` and `UNLINK`. Refusing writes is the right default for data you can't afford to lose. If idempotency keys disappeared without a word, a retried payment would be charged twice. An error at least pages someone.

Two details about the number. The check runs before each command, so the command itself can push memory past the limit: in one run the lab server stopped at 4,218,576 bytes against a limit of 4,194,304. A single command that builds a big value, such as `SUNIONSTORE` over two large sets, can overshoot by far more. And `maxmemory` is compared with what the memory allocator handed out (`used_memory`), not with what the kernel charges the process (`used_memory_rss`, which includes fragmentation). The buffers that feed replicas and the append-only file (Redis's on-disk log of writes, lesson 10) aren't counted at all, and a background save can need extra memory too (lesson 10). So set `maxmemory` well below the container's limit, and graph both numbers.

sections.h: Eviction picks its victim from a small random sample
sections.body:
A cache is allowed to lose entries. A missing card-issuer response only means one slow call to the issuer. So for a cache you want Redis to make room instead of refusing. Which key should go?

The simplest answer is a random one: `allkeys-random`. It treats a merchant profile read 500 times a second the same as one read last Tuesday. The lesson's demo keeps 200 hot keys and reads them before each of four batches of 800 keys that are written once and never read. Under `allkeys-random`, 79 of the 200 hot keys were evicted in one run.

The usual answer is **LRU**, least recently used: evict the key that has gone longest without being read or written. Exact LRU keeps every key in a linked list in order of use and moves a key to the front on every access. That costs two pointers, 16 bytes, per key, plus a list update on every read. With 50 million keys it is 800 MB of pointers, rewritten on the hot path.

Redis approximates it instead. Every key's header has 24 bits for the time of its last access, counted in seconds. When Redis must free memory, it picks 5 keys at random (`maxmemory-samples`), adds them to a pool of the 16 best candidates it has seen so far, and evicts the one that has been idle longest. It repeats until memory is under the limit. Old keys collect in the pool across rounds, so the result is close to true LRU, and 10 samples gets closer still. In the same demo, `allkeys-lru` kept all 200 hot keys, and most of the oldest batch was gone.

Two more families exist. **LFU**, least frequently used (Redis 4.0), replaces the timestamp with an 8-bit counter of how often a key is used. The counter grows logarithmically (about a million reads take it to its maximum, 255) and drops by one for every minute nobody touches the key. A new key starts at 5, so it gets a chance before it is judged. LFU protects popular keys from a one-off scan. A nightly job that reads every key once makes every key look recent to LRU, but under LFU each of those reads adds at most one point, and the hot keys keep their lead. **LRM**, least recently modified (Redis 8.6), updates a key's stamp only on writes, so a key that is read all day but never changed can still go.

Every policy comes as `allkeys-*`, which considers every key, or `volatile-*`, which considers only keys with a TTL. A `volatile-*` policy on a server with no TTL keys behaves exactly like `noeviction`. `volatile-ttl` evicts the key nearest its deadline. Start with `allkeys-lru` for a cache and `noeviction` for data, and keep the two in separate Redis instances.

refs.title: Key eviction: approximated LRU and LFU

analogy: Redis is a small library with one librarian. Some books carry a return-by date. The librarian sets no alarms. When someone asks for a book, she checks its date first, and if it has passed she takes the book away and says it isn't there. Ten times an hour she also walks to a few shelves and pulls out books whose date has passed, more shelves if she keeps finding them, but never for more than a quarter of the hour. When the shelves are full and a new book arrives, either she refuses it (`noeviction`) or she grabs five books at random and removes the one nobody has opened for longest. The analogy breaks on speed and on chance: a real librarian would spot an overdue book right next to the one she pulled, while Redis's sample really is random, and it repeats the whole routine thousands of times a second.
in_your_world: In a payment service, one Redis often ends up holding two kinds of data that want opposite settings. Idempotency keys and rate-limit counters are data: losing one means a duplicate charge or a broken limit, so they need a TTL on every key, `noeviction`, and an alert when `used_memory` gets near `maxmemory`. A cache of card-issuer BIN lookups or merchant profiles may lose anything at any time, so it wants `allkeys-lru` and no alert, because eviction is its normal state. Run them as separate instances with separate settings. Then size the data one: keys alive equals write rate times TTL. At 35 payments a second and a 24-hour TTL that is about 3 million keys. On the lab server 100,000 idempotency keys with a short JSON result took 16.7 MB (167 bytes each, though `MEMORY USAGE` reports 126 for one of them), so 3 million need about 500 MB before any headroom.
mistake: The most common mistake is running a Redis on the defaults: no `maxmemory`, so even `noeviction` never triggers, and the process grows until the container's memory limit kills it and every client loses its connection at once. The second is the reverse: setting `allkeys-lru` on the instance that also holds idempotency keys, sessions or locks. Under memory pressure, Redis evicts whatever has been idle longest, and a 23-hour-old idempotency key is exactly that, so the next retry of that payment finds no key and charges the card again. Both happen because defaults feel safe and one shared Redis feels simple. Decide per instance: data gets a `maxmemory`, `noeviction` and an alert; a cache gets a `maxmemory` and `allkeys-lru`.

worked.title: Size and guard an idempotency store

steps.say: Measure, don't guess. `MEMORY USAGE` reports one key, but it leaves out the key's share of the server's hash tables. Write 100,000 realistic keys and compare `used_memory` before and after. On the lab server that took 16.7 MB, 167 bytes a key, against 126 from `MEMORY USAGE`.

Work out the steady state. With a fixed TTL, the number of live keys stops growing after one TTL: new keys arrive as fast as old ones expire. Live keys = rate × TTL = 35 × 86,400, about 3 million. Times 167 bytes is about 505 MB. Peak days matter more than averages, so size for the busiest day's rate.

Choose the settings. This is data, so `noeviction`. Set `maxmemory` with room above the steady state (here 1 GB) and the container limit with room above `maxmemory` for fragmentation, buffers and saves. Both are plain config lines.

Watch it from the service. A health check that reads `INFO memory` and warns at 80% gives you time to act before writes start failing. With `noeviction`, the first sign of trouble otherwise is a payment that fails with an OOM error.

drill.title: Write chooseVictim from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given `List<String> keys`, `Map<String, Long> lastUsed`, `int samples` and a `Random random`, write `String chooseVictim()` the way Redis approximates LRU. Then compare. Why does Redis sample at all instead of keeping keys in order of use?

alt.src:
fun chooseVictim(): String =
    (1..samples)
        .map { keys[random.nextInt(keys.size)] }                         // a random key, O(1)
        .minBy { lastUsed.getValue(it) }                                 // the oldest of the sample

recap: A TTL is an absolute deadline stored with the key. A plain `SET` drops it; `KEEPTTL` keeps it; `INCR` and `HSET` leave it alone.
Expired keys are deleted lazily when touched, and by a cycle that checks 20 keys at a time, 10 times a second, in slices of at most 25 ms.
An expired key is invisible at once but can stay in memory for a while: 500,000 keys took about 1.1 seconds to reclaim on the lab server.
`maxmemory` defaults to no limit. The default policy, `noeviction`, refuses writes when full and keeps every key.
Eviction samples 5 keys into a pool of 16 candidates and removes the one idle longest (LRU), used least (LFU) or written least recently (LRM, 8.6).
Use `noeviction` for data and `allkeys-lru` for a cache, in separate instances. `volatile-*` policies act like `noeviction` when no key has a TTL.

quiz.q: A key was set with `EX 60`. Thirty seconds later the service runs `SET payment:42:status settled` on it. What does `TTL payment:42:status` return now?
options: About 30
quiz.why: A plain `SET` replaces the value and removes the deadline, so the key no longer has a TTL and `TTL` returns -1. To keep the remaining 30 seconds, the service needed `SET ... KEEPTTL` (or `XX KEEPTTL`). -2 would mean the key doesn't exist, and 60 would need a new `EX 60`.

quiz.q: A Redis has `maxmemory 1gb` and `maxmemory-policy volatile-lru`. It holds only rate-limit counters, none with a TTL, and memory is full. An `INCR` on a new counter arrives. What happens?
options: Redis evicts the least recently used counter and runs the INCR
The INCR fails with an OOM error
Redis grows past 1 GB, because counters are small
Redis evicts a random counter, because no key has a TTL
quiz.why: `volatile-*` policies only consider keys that have a TTL. With none, there is nothing they may evict, so the server behaves like `noeviction` and refuses the write. Redis never falls back to evicting keys without a TTL.

quiz.q: Every night a report job reads every key of a 2-million-key cache once, with `SCAN` and `GET`. The cache runs `allkeys-lru`. What happens to the hot keys during the next morning's evictions?
options: Nothing: LRU knows the hot keys are read thousands of times a day
The scan's reads don't update the LRU stamp, so nothing changes
Redis switches to LFU automatically while a scan runs
They become likely victims: the scan made millions of cold keys look as recent as the hot ones, or more recent
quiz.why: LRU only knows when a key was last used, not how often. The scan stamps every key it reads, so hot keys lose their advantage, and a hot key last read before the scan finished can look older than cold keys the scan touched. `allkeys-lfu` resists this: one read adds at most one point to a counter that hot keys have far above.

quiz.q: A Redis holding 4 GB of idempotency keys keeps `used_memory` just under `maxmemory 4gb`, but the container (limit 4.2 GB) gets killed with exit code 137 during a background save. Why?
options: `maxmemory` limits what the allocator handed out; the kernel counts the process's real memory, which also includes fragmentation, buffers and the save's extra pages
`maxmemory` only applies to keys with a TTL
`noeviction` lets Redis grow past `maxmemory` during saves
Exit code 137 means Redis ran out of disk space
quiz.why: Redis compares `maxmemory` with `used_memory`, the allocator's count. The kernel kills the process based on its resident memory (`used_memory_rss` and more), which adds fragmentation, replica and AOF buffers, and pages copied during a background save (lesson 10). Leave headroom between `maxmemory` and the container's limit. Exit code 137 means the process received SIGKILL, here from the out-of-memory killer.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: 500,000 keys expire in the same second. Where does the work of deleting them happen, and what does a client's GET on an unrelated key see?
options: On a background thread, so the GET is unaffected
On the main thread, in slices of at most 25 ms, so the GET can wait up to one slice
On the main thread, all at once, so the GET waits until all 500,000 are gone
In a forked child process, like a snapshot
quiz.why: The active expiry cycle runs on the one thread that executes every command, between commands. It caps each run at 25% of the 100 ms tick, so other clients are served between the slices, but a GET that arrives during one waits for it. With the default `lazyfree-lazy-expire no`, the freeing happens on the main thread too.

flashcards.front: What does a plain `SET` do to an existing key's TTL?
flashcards.back: Removes it: the key lives forever. `SET ... KEEPTTL` (Redis 6.0) keeps the old deadline.

flashcards.front: What are Redis's two ways of expiring keys?
flashcards.back: Lazy: every access checks the deadline and deletes an expired key. Active: a cycle checks 20 keys with a TTL at a time, 10 times a second.

flashcards.front: When does the active expiry cycle go again at once, and when does it stop?
flashcards.back: It repeats while more than 10% of a batch had expired, and stops after 25 ms, a quarter of the 100 ms tick.

flashcards.front: What does a full Redis do under the default `noeviction`?
flashcards.back: Refuses commands that add data with `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'`. Reads and deletes still work.
It samples `maxmemory-samples` keys (5) into a pool of 16 candidates and evicts the one idle longest, by a 24-bit, one-second stamp in each key.

flashcards.front: What does `volatile-lru` do when no key has a TTL?
flashcards.back: Nothing: it behaves like `noeviction` and writes fail with an OOM error.

flashcards.front: LRU, LFU or LRM: which ignores reads?
flashcards.back: LRM, least recently modified (Redis 8.6). It updates a key's stamp only on writes.

terms.plain: Time to live: how long until a key's deadline. `TTL` returns -1 for no deadline and -2 for no key.
Deleting an expired key when a command touches it, before the command runs.
A cycle on the main thread that checks keys with a deadline and deletes the expired ones, 10 times a second.
The memory limit Redis compares `used_memory` with before each write. 0, the default, means no limit.
What Redis does at `maxmemory`: refuse writes (`noeviction`) or delete keys chosen by LRU, LFU, LRM, TTL or at random.
Least recently used: evict the key that has gone longest without a read or write.
Least frequently used: evict the key with the lowest access counter, a logarithmic 8-bit count that decays over time.
Redis's list of the 16 best eviction candidates seen so far, kept across evictions.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate set `EX 86400` on idempotency keys and is surprised that `DBSIZE` sometimes counts keys whose 24 hours are up, and that writes started failing once the instance filled up. Explain both, and what you'd change.
explain_back.answer: Redis doesn't delete a key at its deadline. Every command that touches a key checks the deadline first and deletes it then, so no client ever reads an expired key. Keys nobody touches are removed by a cycle that runs 10 times a second and checks 20 keys with a TTL at a time, going on while it keeps finding expired ones, for at most 25 ms per run. Until that cycle reaches a key, it still takes memory and still counts in `DBSIZE`. The failing writes come from the eviction policy. At `maxmemory` the default, `noeviction`, refuses writes instead of deleting anything. For idempotency keys that is right, because losing one could charge a card twice. So I'd keep `noeviction`, size `maxmemory` for write rate times TTL with room to spare, alert when `used_memory` passes 80% of it, and move any cache data to a separate instance with `allkeys-lru`.

deeper.body:
The active cycle has a second, faster mode. Before the event loop goes back to sleep, Redis may run a "fast" expiry cycle that lasts at most 1 ms. It runs only when Redis estimates that at least 10% of the keys with a TTL are already expired, or when the last slow run hit its time limit. The slow cycle in the 10-times-a-second timer does the bulk of the work. `active-expire-effort` (1 to 10, default 1) raises the batch size, the time budget and the acceptable stale share together: at 10, each batch checks 65 keys, a run may use 43% of the tick, and the cycle keeps going until only 1% of a batch is expired.

The freeing itself happens on the main thread unless you say otherwise. `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes` hands expired values to the `bio_lazy_free` background thread from lesson 1, and `lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes` does the same for evicted keys. That matters when keys are big: expiring one hash with a million fields frees a lot of memory in one go.

The 24-bit LRU stamp counts seconds and wraps after 2^24 seconds, about 194 days. Redis handles the wrap when it computes idle time, so a key idle for longer than that just looks less idle than it is. `OBJECT IDLETIME` shows the idle time in seconds, which is why it rarely shows anything but small numbers on a busy key.

One surprise while testing the eviction lab: a Lua script is checked against `maxmemory` only when it starts. If the server was over the limit then, the script's first write fails. Once a script has written anything, Redis lets it run to the end, because stopping it halfway would break its atomicity (lesson 6). A script that began under the limit wrote 100,000 keys of 1 KB into a server with `maxmemory 4mb`, and `used_memory` ended at 108 MB. A client that loops over `SET` sees the OOM error on time; one script can blow straight through the limit.

`maxmemory-eviction-tenacity` (default 10) limits how long one command may spend evicting before Redis moves the rest of the work to a background timer, so a burst of big writes can't stall one client for long. Set `maxmemory-clients` if a few clients with huge buffers could crowd out the data.
